changes.current_line: Online and in-store on one platform; the line between them has pretty much disappeared.
changes.change: For retail store and operations buyers, replace the line with: "One system for the tills and the website." "one customer, one basket." Back it with a live, step-by-step demo of an online order being returned at a store till, not a slide. Say "the tills" instead of "point of sale" or "in-person payments" with this audience.
changes.why: M3 was presented from a slide and dismissed as "that's a diagram." The buyer then asked for a till return step by step, which we described but never showed, and the customer's own words for the need were sharper than ours.

changes.change: For retail COO and store-operations buyers, add a single-accountability line: one team owns the store rollout, the installs and the Saturday till outage, named by role, under one contract if we can offer it. Address the fear directly: no "two vendors pointing at each other."
changes.why: The decider said "I don't want two vendors pointing at each other." Adyen reportedly offered one platform on one contract with a store-rollout team, and our answer that a partner would do the installs ended the store team's questions.

changes.current_line: Trusted by leading businesses; see our customer stories.
changes.change: For retail buyers, back the proof line with retailer references the buyer can call, available on short notice, plus a template rollout plan covering dates, who installs, and what happens to the old tills. Do not rely on written customer stories alone with this buyer.
changes.why: The decider asked "can I talk to them?" and we could not set up a call in time. She also wanted a dated rollout plan, while Adyen named retailers she knew.

changes.change: For retailers, add an opener built on the store-side failure: an order bought online and returned in store, where the store cannot see the order because store and web are two different customer records. Lead with this before any global or currency framing.
changes.why: The trigger was a buy-online, return-in-store failure caused by split customer records, and the origin story centred on the COO in a store watching the returns queue, not on checkout.
